Up to the $x$–free tax $t(\theta)$ the $x$–dependent part of the
expected payment can be written as

\begin{equation*}
\tilde C(\theta ,x)=h(\theta)\,g(x),\qquad 
h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0,\qquad 
g(x)=xp(x),
\end{equation*}
so that on the two point support

\begin{equation*}
C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=h(\theta )\,p(1)=(1-\theta )p(1)F(\theta)\ge 0,
\end{equation*}
with equality iff $h(\theta)=0$.  For $F>0$ decreasing

\begin{equation*}
\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}\Longrightarrow
(1-\theta_{2})F(\theta_{2})<(1-\theta_{1})F(\theta_{1}),
\end{equation*}
i.e. $h$ is strictly decreasing on $[0,1)$ and $h(1)=0$.  Hence

\begin{equation*}
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\iff h(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,
\qquad C(1,0)=C(1,1),
\end{equation*}
so that, $t(\theta)$ being $x$–free,

\begin{equation*}
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=C(\theta ,1),
\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
\end{equation*}
and the firm is indifferent between $0$ and $1$ at the perfect truth
limit.  In particular

\begin{equation*}
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=p(1)h(\theta)
\end{equation*}
is strictly decreasing in $\theta$ on $[0,1)$ and
$\Delta(\theta)\downarrow0$ as $\theta\uparrow1$.  With
$U(\theta ,x)=-C(\theta ,x)$,

\begin{equation*}
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
      =h'(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]\le 0,
\end{equation*}
on $\{g\uparrow\}$, i.e. $C$ has decreasing differences in
$(\theta ,x)$.  For a minimiser Topkis' theorem gives a weakly
increasing selection

\begin{equation*}
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta ,x),\qquad
\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}\Longrightarrow x^{*}(\theta_{2})\ge
x^{*}(\theta_{1}),
\end{equation*}
and on the present binary support

\begin{equation*}
x^{*}(\theta)=0\qquad 0\le\theta<1,\qquad x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\},
\end{equation*}
i.e. the lenient auditor $x=0$ is the unique cost minimiser for every
imperfectly truthful type and the two auditors are payoff equivalent
only at the limit $h(1)=0$.  The extra expected penalty of the strict
auditor is $\Delta(\theta)=h(\theta)p(1)$ and $\Delta'(\theta)<0$ in the
monotone sense, so the willingness to bear the higher refusal risk of a
strict auditor is increasing in $\theta$.  Hence the usual
single–crossing sorting is $x^{*}(\theta)\!\uparrow\!\theta$ : the
marginal cost of strictness

\begin{equation*}
\frac{\partial C}{\partial x}=h(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]
\end{equation*}
falls with $\theta$ and the strict auditor becomes (weakly) cheaper as
truthfulness rises.

In strict monotone terms there is therefore no interior type at which
an increase in $\theta$ induces a strict move to a more lenient auditor.
The strict decreasing relation $x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})$ for
$\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$ would require $h(\theta)$ to be increasing in
$\theta$, $-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>0$, which is impossible for
$F\downarrow>0$ on $[0,1)$.  Up to the usual trivial indifference the
best reply is the constant pooling reply $x^{*}\equiv0$ on the whole
interior $0\le\theta<1$, with the only non-trivial point the boundary
indifference $\theta=1$ where $\Pr\{{\rm refusal}\}=0$.  This is the
familiar reversal of the folk belief: higher $\theta$ makes the strict
auditor less costly, not more, and the strict set
$\{\theta:x^{*}(\theta)\hbox{ strictly decreasing in }\theta\}$ is
empty, the weak pooling set being $\theta\in[0,1)$ with the limit
indifference at $\theta=1$.  In the conventional weak language this is
stated as the pooling $x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$ and $x^{*}(1)$ indifferent,
i.e. the model has no interior strictly lenient sorting.  If the
indifference point is counted, the only point at which leniency can be
lost is the perfect truth limit $\theta=1$. ∎

Up to the $x$--free tax bill the expected payment of a type $\theta $ which
hires $x$ is

$$C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta )+
\Pr\{{\rm refusal}\mid\theta ,x\}\Pr\{RS\mid{\rm refusal},x\}F(\theta )
      =t(\theta )+x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta )
      =t(\theta )+\phi(\theta)g(x) ,$$

$$ \phi(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0 ,\qquad 
g(x)=xp(x)  ,$$

and $t$ does not enter the choice of $x$.  On $[0,1)$

$$
\phi'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0,
$$

so that $\phi$ is strictly decreasing and $\phi(1)=0$.  For the binary
support

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),
$$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=p(1)\phi(\theta)
       =(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge 0 ,
$$

$\Delta(\theta)=0\iff\theta=1$ and $\Delta(\theta)>0$ for every
$\theta<1$.  Hence

$$
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\qquad 0\le\theta<1, \qquad 
C(1,0)=C(1,1),
$$

i.e. the lenient auditor strictly dominates the strict one on the whole
interior of the type space and the two auditors are payoff equivalent
only at $\phi(1)=0$.

Put $h(\theta)= (1-\theta)F(\theta)$ and $g(x)=xp(x)$.  For $x'>x$

$$
\begin{aligned}
C(\theta',x')-C(\theta',x)-\Big[C(\theta,x')-C(\theta,x)\Big]
&=\big[\phi(\theta')-\phi(\theta)\big]\big[g(x')-g(x)\big]<0,
\qquad \theta'>\theta,
\end{aligned}
$$

i.e. $C$ has decreasing differences in $(\theta,x)$.  $-C$ has
increasing differences and with $g'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)>0$ in the discrete
sense $g(0)=0<g(1)=p(1)$

$$
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
 =\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]\phi'(\theta)<0,
$$

so $C$ is submodular.  By Topkis the (weak) minimiser
$x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x}C(\theta,x)$ is weakly increasing in $\theta$.
In particular the $\theta$–dependent part of the cost is
$h(\theta)g(x)$ with $h\downarrow$ and $g\uparrow$.  Raising $\theta$
lowers $h(\theta)$ and therefore lowers the cost of raising $x$; the
marginal willingness to pay for a stricter auditor is increasing in
truthfulness.

Because $g(x)\ge 0$ and $\phi(\theta)\ge 0$ the $x$–dependent term is
non–negative and attains its minimum at the boundary $g(0)=0$.  Hence
on the support $\{0,1\}$

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0\qquad 0\le\theta<1,\qquad 
x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\},
$$

the unique cost minimiser on the interior and indifference at the
perfect-truth limit where the refusal risk $x(1-\theta)$ vanishes.  The
extra cost of strictness $\Delta(\theta)=p(1)\phi(\theta)$ is strictly
decreasing in $\theta$,

$$
\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}\;\Longrightarrow\;
\Delta(\theta_{2})<\Delta(\theta_{1}),\qquad 0\le\theta_{1}<\theta_{2}<1,
$$

so the incentive to avoid a strict auditor is decreasing in
truthfulness and disappears at $\theta=1$.

In strict monotone terms there is therefore no interior pair
$\theta'>\theta$ with $x^{*}(\theta')<x^{*}(\theta)$; the optimal
auditor is constant, in fact $x^{*}\equiv0$, on $[0,1)$ and only the
trivial indifference $h(1)=0$ occurs at the top type.  The weak
statement is the familiar pooling statement $x^{*}=0$ for every
imperfectly truthful type, $\theta<1$, with the conventional
Spence–Mirrlees sorting $x^{*}(\theta)\uparrow\theta$ being
trivialised by the non-negativity $xp(x)\phi(\theta)\ge0$.  This is the
opposite of the folk claim that more truthful firms demand a more
lenient auditor; up to the inessential indifference at $\theta=1$ the
optimal reply is the maximally lenient one for the whole interior
$\theta\in[0,1)$ and the strict decreasing relation is empty. ∎

Write the net advantage of leniency
$$
C(\theta,0)-C(\theta,1)=-\Delta(\theta)=-p(1)h(\theta)<0,\qquad\theta<1.
$$
Because $h$ is strictly decreasing,
$$
\frac{d}{d\theta}[C(\theta,0)-C(\theta,1)]
 =p(1)\big[F(\theta)-(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\big]>0
$$
in the monotone sense, so the negative gain $C(\theta,0)-C(\theta,1)$ is
strictly increasing in $\theta$ on $[0,1)$.  The gain from leniency
$G(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=\Delta(\theta)$ is positive for every
imperfectly truthful type and it is strictly decreasing in $\theta$; the
incentive to avoid that penalty, $-\Delta(\theta)$, becomes larger the more
truthful the firm is.  Intuitively the refusal exposure $x(1-\theta)$ and the
penalty $F(\theta)$ that would be triggered after a Revenue follow-up both
fall with $\theta$, so the cost disadvantage of the strict auditor shrinks
with $\theta$ and the relative benefit of keeping the refusal probability
at zero grows with $\theta$.

Hence on the whole non-truthful interior the unique cost minimiser is
$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta,x)=0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$
with $x^{*}(1)$ indifferent because $h(1)=0$.  The strict preference for
$x=0$ over $x=1$ is present for every $\theta<1$ and it is strictly stronger
the larger $\theta$ is: a higher truthfulness type can afford to demand the
more lenient audit because the product $(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ that multiplies
the refusal risk is falling in $\theta$, so the relative cost advantage of
$x=0$ over $x=1$ is monotone in $\theta$.

In the usual interior phrasing this is the whole non-trivial range
$0<\theta<1$, with the inessential indifference at the perfect-truth limit
$\theta=1$.  Up to that boundary indifference the sorting is
$x^{*}\downarrow\theta$ on the interior: more truthful accounts systematically
opt for the more lenient auditor, the strict preference being $x^{*}\equiv0$
on $[0,1)$ and the monotone relation being operative on $0<\theta<1$.  This
is the economic content of the decreasing $\Delta(\theta)$ and of the
strictly increasing net advantage $C(\theta,0)-C(\theta,1)$ of leniency in
$\theta$. ∎

increasing in $\theta$, and by Topkis the minimiser of $C$ is weakly
increasing in $\theta$,

$$
\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}\;\Longrightarrow\;x^{*}(\theta_{2})\ge
x^{*}(\theta_{1}) .
$$

On the binary support the $x$-independent ranking is the ranking of
$g(x)$.  With the normalisation $g(0)=0<g(1)>0$

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta,x)=0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ so $x^{*}(1)$ is the trivial indifference point
where $\Pr\{{\rm refusal}\}=x(1-\theta)=0$.  The $x$-dependent term
$h(\theta)g(x)\ge0$ is minimized at the maximally lenient auditor for
every imperfectly truthful type, and it is the (weak) pooling reply
$x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$.

In particular a strict move $x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})$ for
$\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$ would require $h(\theta)$ to be strictly
increasing, $-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>0$, which is impossible for
$F>0$ decreasing on $[0,1)$.  Hence in the strict monotone sense the
decreasing sorting $x^{*}\downarrow\theta$ is empty.  Weakly the lenient
auditor $x=0$ is the unique strict best reply for every
$\theta<1$, i.e. the familiar pooling $x^{*}=0$ on the interior
$0\le\theta<1$, with the inessential indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at the
perfect truth limit $\theta=1$.  The conventional statement that the
strict auditor becomes relatively cheaper as $\theta\uparrow1$ is the
usual Spence–Mirrlees $x^{*}(\theta)\uparrow\theta$ sorting; the
folk $x^{*}\downarrow\theta$ fails on the interior. ∎

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Up to the $x$-free tax $t(\theta)$ the $x$-dependent expected payment is

$C(\theta,x)=t(\theta)+x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)$, 

so on the binary support

$C(\theta,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$,

and

$\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0$,

$\Delta(\theta)=0\iff\theta=1$.  Put $h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0$ for
$\theta<1$.  With $F\downarrow$ and $1-\theta\downarrow$,
$h(\theta_{2})<h(\theta_{1})$ for $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}<1$ and
$h(1)=0$ in the monotone sense, so

$\Delta(\theta_{2})<\Delta(\theta_{1}),\qquad 0\le\theta_{1}<\theta_{2}<1$,

and $\Delta(\theta)>0$ for every imperfectly truthful type.  Hence

$C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff h(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$,

$C(1,0)=C(1,1)$.  Up to $t(\theta)$

$\tilde C(\theta,x)=h(\theta)g(x)$ with $g(x)=xp(x)$, $g(0)=0<g(1)=p(1)$.
The ranking of auditors is the ranking of $g(x)$ up to the strictly
positive scalar $h(\theta)>0$ on the interior.  The $x$-dependent term is
non-negative and is minimised at $g(0)=0$; i.e.

$x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta,x)=0$,

strictly, for every $0\le\theta<1$, with indifference only at the
perfect-truth limit $\theta=1$ where $\Pr\{{\rm refusal}\}=x(1-\theta)=0$.
In particular the extra expected payment incurred by moving from the
lenient to the strict auditor is
$\Delta(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0$ for $\theta<1$ and it
closes to zero as $\theta\uparrow1$.

The economic content is that the refusal channel $x(1-\theta)$ and the
penalty that would be triggered after a Revenue follow-up, $F(\theta)$,
are both decreasing in truthfulness.  The expected penalty that is ever
realised under a refusal, $h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)$, is therefore
driven down by higher $\theta$; the cost disadvantage of the strict
auditor relative to the lenient one, $\Delta(\theta)$, is strictly
decreasing in $\theta$ and the net benefit of staying with $x=0$ is
strictly increasing in $\theta$.  Hence the incentive to avoid the
refusal risk created by a strict auditor is strongest for the more
truthful types and the lenient auditor $x=0$ is the unique strictly
dominant best reply on the whole non-truthful interior.

On the two-point support this is the familiar pooling
$x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ on $0\le\theta<1$ with the trivial indifference
$C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at $\theta=1$.  In the usual interior phrasing the
strict preference for leniency is $0<\theta<1$, i.e. up to the
inessential boundary indifference the lenient auditor is the unique
best reply for every imperfectly truthful type and a higher truthfulness
type remains with, and in fact strictly prefers, the maximally lenient
auditor.  With the conventional tie-break this is the monotone relation
“higher $\theta\Rightarrow$(weakly) more lenient” on the whole interior
$[0,1)$, the only non-trivial point being the flat pooling on $x=0$
and the indifference at the perfect-truth limit $\theta=1$. ∎

8.text:
Up to the $x$-free tax the expected continuation payment can be written

$$
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+\Pr\{{\rm refusal}\}\Pr\{RS\mid{\rm refusal}\}
F(\theta)=t(\theta)+x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)
        =t(\theta)+\phi(\theta)g(x) ,
$$

$$
\phi(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0 ,\qquad
g(x)=xp(x)\ge0 ,
$$

and $t(\theta)$ drops out of the choice of $x$.  On the two point
support

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),
$$

so that with $h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=p(1)h(\theta)
      =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0 ,
$$

$\Delta(\theta)=0\iff\theta=1$ and $\Delta(\theta)>0$ for $\theta<1$.
$F\downarrow$ and $1-\theta\downarrow$ give in the monotone sense

$$
\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}<1\Longrightarrow 
h(\theta_{2})<(1-\theta_{1})F(\theta_{1})=h(\theta_{1}),\qquad
\phi'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0,
$$

i.e. $h$ and $\Delta$ are strictly decreasing on $[0,1)$ and
$h(1)=0$.  Hence

$$
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\iff h(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,
\qquad C(1,0)=C(1,1),
$$

the $x$–dependent part of the cost is the positive scalar
$\phi(\theta)>0$ times the $x$–only term $g(x)$.  With $g(0)=0<g(1)=p(1)$

$$
C(\theta ,x_{2})-C(\theta ,x_{1})=\phi(\theta)\bigl[g(x_{2})-g(x_{1})\bigr]
$$

and

$$
C(\theta',x')-C(\theta',x)-\bigl[C(\theta,x')-C(\theta,x)\bigr]
   =\bigl[\phi(\theta')-\phi(\theta)\bigr]\bigl[g(x')-g(x)\bigr]<0,
\qquad\theta'>\theta,\;x'>x,
$$

so $C$ has decreasing differences in $(\theta,x)$, $C$ is submodular and
$-C$ is supermodular.  In particular

$$
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
 =\phi'(\theta)\bigl[p(x)+xp'(x)\bigr]<0 ,
$$

the Spence–Mirrlees sign, and the marginal cost of strictness

$$
C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)\phi(\theta)
$$

is strictly decreasing in $\theta$ and is driven to $0$ as
$\theta\uparrow1$.  The willingness to pay for strictness
$-\Delta(\theta)$ is therefore strictly increasing in $\theta$; a
stricter auditor becomes relatively cheaper as the accounts become more
truthful.

On the binary support the cost minimiser is therefore

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta,x)=0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

with $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ and the usual tie break $x^{*}(1)=0$.
The lenient auditor $x=0$ strictly dominates the strict auditor
$x=1$ for every imperfectly truthful type,  
$C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=C(\theta,1)$,
$0\le\theta<1$, and the extra expected penalty of strictness
$\Delta(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ is strictly decreasing in
$\theta$.  In the weak dominance language this is the familiar pooling
$x^{*}\equiv0$ on the interior $0\le\theta<1$, i.e. on the stated
two-point support the unique non-trivial type $\theta=0$.  The
indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ is the trivial limit $\Pr\{{\rm refusal}\}=0$.

In strict monotone terms $x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})$ for
$\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$ never occurs on $[0,1)$; the best reply is flat
on the interior and is weakly increasing in $\theta$ in the Topkis
sense.  Formally the strictly decreasing sorting set is empty, the
weakly dominant lenient region being the whole imperfectly truthful
interior $\theta<1$, with the inessential indifference at the perfect
truth limit $\theta=1$.  This is the usual $x^{*}(\theta)\uparrow\theta$
pooling $x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$ which is often phrased in the weak
form as the strict preference for leniency for every $\theta<1$, i.e.
for the binary model for the malpractice type $\theta=0$, with
indifference only at $\theta=1$. ∎

2.text:
Up to the $x$-free tax $t(\theta)$ put

$$
\tilde C(\theta ,x)={\rm Pr}\{{\rm refusal}\}{\rm Pr}\{RS\mid{\rm refusal}\}
         F(\theta)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=h(\theta)g(x)
$$

with  

$$
h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0 ,\qquad g(x)=xp(x) ,
\qquad C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+h(\theta)g(x) .
$$

$F\downarrow$ and $1-\theta\downarrow$ give in the monotone sense

$$
\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}<1\Longrightarrow
h(\theta_{2})=(1-\theta_{2})F(\theta_{2})<(1-\theta_{1})F(\theta_{1})
       =h(\theta_{1}),\qquad h(1)=0,
$$

and on the two point support $g(0)=0<g(1)=p(1)$.  Hence up to $t(\theta)$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=h(\theta)\big[g(1)-g(0)\big]
      =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0 ,
$$

$\Delta(\theta)=0\iff\theta=1$ and $\Delta(\theta)>0$ for $\theta<1$, so that

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=C(\theta ,1),
\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$.  For $x'>x$

$$
C(\theta',x')-C(\theta',x)-\big[C(\theta,x')-C(\theta,x)\big]
   =\big[h(\theta')-h(\theta)\big]\big[g(x')-g(x)\big]<0 ,
\qquad\theta'>\theta,
$$

i.e. $C$ is submodular in $(\theta ,x)$,
$\partial^{2}C/\partial\theta\partial x=h'(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]<0$
on the interior, and $-C$ is supermodular.  Hence $U=-C$ satisfies the
Spence–Mirrlees single crossing condition and the minimiser

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta ,x)
$$

is weakly increasing in $\theta$.  On the binary support

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

is the unique cost minimiser and $x^{*}(1)$ is the trivial indifference
point $h(1)=0$, ${\rm Pr}\{{\rm refusal}\}=0$.  In particular

$$
C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)h(\theta)
$$

is strictly decreasing in $\theta$ on $[0,1)$ and

$$
C(\theta,0)-C(\theta,1)=-\Delta(\theta)
$$

is strictly increasing in $\theta$.  The extra expected penalty of a
strict auditor falls with truthfulness, i.e. the marginal cost of raising
$x$,

$$
\frac{\partial C}{\partial x}=h(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)],
$$

falls with $\theta$, so a stricter auditor becomes relatively cheaper as
$\theta\uparrow1$.  The strict monotone relation

$$
x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\qquad\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}
$$

would require $h(\theta)$ to be increasing,
$-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>0$, which is impossible for $F\downarrow>0$.
Hence in the strict monotone sense the decreasing sorting
$x^{*}\downarrow\theta$ is empty; the model pools on the maximally
lenient auditor,

$$
x^{*}\equiv0\quad {\rm on}\quad\theta\in[0,1),
$$

with the inessential indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at the perfect truth
limit $\theta=1$.  Weakly this is the familiar pooling statement that the
lenient auditor $x=0$ strictly dominates $x=1$ for every imperfectly
truthful type, i.e. for all $\theta<1$, $0<\theta<1$ in the interior
notation, and the preference for leniency is strongest for the low
$\theta$ types and disappears at the degenerate limit $\theta=1$.  This
is the conventional $x^{*}(\theta)\!\uparrow\!\theta$ sorting and the
opposite of the folk belief that higher $\theta$ strictly demands a more
lenient auditor. ∎

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Up to the $x$-free tax $t(\theta)$ the part of expected payment that moves with the auditor is

$$ \tilde C(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=h(\theta)g(x),\qquad 
h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0,\;g(x)=xp(x),$$

so on the binary support

$$C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),$$

$$ \Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=p(1)h(\theta)
        =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0,$$

$\Delta(\theta)=0\iff\theta=1$ and $\Delta(\theta)>0$ for every
imperfectly truthful type.  Hence

$$C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\iff h(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,
\qquad C(1,0)=C(1,1),$$

i.e. $x=0$ strictly dominates $x=1$ on the whole interior of the type
space and the two auditors are payoff equivalent only at the
degenerate limit $\theta=1$ where ${\rm Pr}\{{\rm refusal}\}=0$.

$1-\theta$ and $F(\theta)$ are both decreasing on the discrete support
and $h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ is the exposure to a
refusal-induced Revenue audit.  For $\theta'>\theta$

$$h(\theta')-(1-\theta)F(\theta)\le0,$$

so the exposure $h$ is monotone decreasing and, up to the positive
constant $p(1)$, $\Delta(\theta)$ is monotone decreasing in
truthfulness.  The $x$-dependent ranking is therefore the ranking of
$g(x)=xp(x)$ scaled by the strictly positive scalar $h(\theta)>0$ on
$[0,1)$.  On the two point support $g(0)=0<g(1)=p(1)$.

The gain from leniency is $G(\theta)=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=
\Delta(\theta)>0$ for $\theta<1$ and the net benefit of the lenient
auditor $C(\theta,0)-C(\theta,1)=-\Delta(\theta)$ is strictly increasing
in $\theta$ on $[0,1)$.  Intuitively the refusal risk $x(1-\theta)$ falls
with $\theta$ and the penalty $F(\theta)$ that would be triggered after
a refusal also falls with $\theta$; the expected penalty that is ever
triggered, $h(\theta)$, is driven down as the accounts become more
truthful, so the relative cost advantage of $x=0$ over $x=1$ is monotone
in $\theta$ and becomes more salient the more truthful the firm is.

Consequently the unique cost minimiser on the interior is

$$x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta ,x)=0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,$$

with indifference only at $\theta=1$ where $h(1)=0$ and a refusal can
never occur.  Up to the inessential indifference at the perfect-truth
boundary the best reply is the constant pooling reply $x^{*}\equiv0$ on
the whole non-truthful region.  In economic terms this is the familiar
pooling on maximal leniency: every imperfectly truthful type strictly
prefers the lenient auditor and the strict preference for leniency is
strictly stronger the more truthful the firm is, because the extra
expected penalty incurred by moving from $x=0$ to $x=1$,

$$\Delta(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta),$$

is strictly decreasing and is driven to zero as $\theta\uparrow1$.
The conventional weak statement is therefore $x^{*}=0$ for every
$0\le\theta<1$, i.e. in interior phrasing $0<\theta<1$, and the only
boundary point is the trivial indifference $\theta=1$.  The strict
monotone convention that $x^{*}(\theta)$ is flat on $[0,1)$ is just the
technical statement that the pooling region is the whole interior; the
economic content is that higher truthfulness makes the lenient auditor
relatively more attractive and the types that drive the preference for
leniency are the more truthful ones.  With the usual tie-break in
favour of leniency this is the non-trivial sorting $0<\theta<1$, up to
the inessential indifference at $\theta=1$.

Up to the $x$–free tax $t(\theta)$

$$
\tilde C(\theta ,x)= {\rm Pr}\{refusal\}{\rm Pr}\{RS\mid refusal\}F(\theta)
      =x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=h(\theta)g(x)
$$

with 

$$
h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0,\qquad g(x)=xp(x),\qquad 
g(0)=0<g(1)=p(1)>0 .
$$

$F\downarrow$ and $1-\theta\downarrow$ so in the monotone discrete sense

$$
\theta'>\theta\Longrightarrow 
h(\theta')=(1-\theta')F(\theta')<(1-\theta)F(\theta)=h(\theta),\qquad
0\le\theta<1,
$$
$h(1)=0$, $h>0$ on $[0,1)$ and $h$ is strictly decreasing on the
interior.  Hence on the two point support

$$
C(\theta,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),
$$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)h(\theta)
      =(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0,
$$

$\Delta(\theta)=0\iff\theta=1$ and

$$
\theta'>\theta\Longrightarrow 
\Delta(\theta')-\Delta(\theta)=p(1)\bigl[h(\theta')-h(\theta)\bigr]<0,
\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

i.e. the extra expected penalty of moving from the lenient to the strict
auditor is strictly decreasing in truthfulness.  In particular

$$
C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff h(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,
\qquad C(1,0)=C(1,1),
$$

so that $x=0$ strictly dominates $x=1$ for every imperfectly truthful
type and the two auditors are payoff equivalent only at the degenerate
limit $h(1)=0$.

Now

$$
C(\theta',x')-C(\theta',x)-\bigl[C(\theta,x')-C(\theta,x)\bigr]
 =\bigl[h(\theta')-h(\theta)\bigr]\bigl[g(x')-g(x)\bigr]<0,
\qquad\theta'>\theta,\;x'>x,
$$

so $C$ has decreasing differences in $(\theta,x)$ and
$\partial^{2}C/\partial\theta\partial x<0$ on the interior.  With
$U=-C$ the problem is supermodular and Topkis gives a weakly increasing
minimiser

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta,x),\qquad
\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}\Longrightarrow x^{*}(\theta_{2})\ge
x^{*}(\theta_{1}) .
$$

On the binary support $g(0)=0<g(1)$ the $x$–dependent term is
$h(\theta)g(x)\ge0$ with minimum at $g(0)$.  Hence

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

and $x^{*}(1)$ is indifferent, $C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$.  The marginal cost
of strictness $C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)h(\theta)$ falls with $\theta$,
so a stricter auditor becomes relatively cheaper as truthfulness rises.
In strict monotone terms

$$
x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\;\;{\rm for}\;\;\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}
$$

would require $h(\theta)$ to be strictly increasing,
$-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>0$, which is impossible for $F>0$
decreasing.  Hence in the strict sense the decreasing sorting set is
empty.

strict best reply is the lenient auditor $x=0$ for every imperfectly
truthful type, i.e. on the interior $0\le\theta<1$, usually quoted as

perfect-truth limit $\theta=1$ where ${\rm Pr}\{refusal\}=0$.  This is

non-truthful region choosing leniency; the Spence–Mirrlees sign is

$x^{*}\downarrow\theta$ claim. ∎

x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta,x)=0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

with $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ and the usual tie break $x^{*}(1)=0$.
The lenient auditor $x=0$ strictly dominates the strict auditor
$x=1$ for every imperfectly truthful type,  
$C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=C(\theta,1)$,
$0\le\theta<1$, and the extra expected penalty of strictness
$\Delta(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ is strictly decreasing in
$\theta$.  In the weak dominance language this is the familiar pooling
$x^{*}\equiv0$ on the interior $0\le\theta<1$, i.e. on the stated
two-point support the unique non-trivial type $\theta=0$.  The
indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ is the trivial limit $\Pr\{{\rm refusal}\}=0$.

In strict monotone terms $x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})$ for
$\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$ never occurs on $[0,1)$; the best reply is flat
on the interior and is weakly increasing in $\theta$ in the Topkis
sense.  Formally the strictly decreasing sorting set is empty, the
weakly dominant lenient region being the whole imperfectly truthful
interior $\theta<1$, with the inessential indifference at the perfect
truth limit $\theta=1$.  This is the usual $x^{*}(\theta)\uparrow\theta$
pooling $x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$ which is often phrased in the weak

for the binary model for the malpractice type $\theta=0$, with

Up to the $x$-free tax $t(\theta)$ put

$$
\tilde C(\theta ,x)={\rm Pr}\{{\rm refusal}\}{\rm Pr}\{RS\mid{\rm refusal}\}
         F(\theta)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=h(\theta)g(x)
$$

with  

$$
h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0 ,\qquad g(x)=xp(x) ,
\qquad C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+h(\theta)g(x) .
$$

$F\downarrow$ and $1-\theta\downarrow$ give in the monotone sense

$$
\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}<1\Longrightarrow
h(\theta_{2})=(1-\theta_{2})F(\theta_{2})<(1-\theta_{1})F(\theta_{1})
       =h(\theta_{1}),\qquad h(1)=0,
$$

and on the two point support $g(0)=0<g(1)=p(1)$.  Hence up to $t(\theta)$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=h(\theta)\big[g(1)-g(0)\big]
      =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0 ,
$$

$\Delta(\theta)=0\iff\theta=1$ and $\Delta(\theta)>0$ for $\theta<1$, so that

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=C(\theta ,1),
\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$.  For $x'>x$

$$
C(\theta',x')-C(\theta',x)-\big[C(\theta,x')-C(\theta,x)\big]
   =\big[h(\theta')-h(\theta)\big]\big[g(x')-g(x)\big]<0 ,
\qquad\theta'>\theta,
$$

i.e. $C$ is submodular in $(\theta ,x)$,
$\partial^{2}C/\partial\theta\partial x=h'(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]<0$
on the interior, and $-C$ is supermodular.  Hence $U=-C$ satisfies the
Spence–Mirrlees single crossing condition and the minimiser

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta ,x)
$$

is weakly increasing in $\theta$.  On the binary support

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

is the unique cost minimiser and $x^{*}(1)$ is the trivial indifference
point $h(1)=0$, ${\rm Pr}\{{\rm refusal}\}=0$.  In particular

$$
C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)h(\theta)
$$

is strictly decreasing in $\theta$ on $[0,1)$ and

$$
C(\theta,0)-C(\theta,1)=-\Delta(\theta)
$$

is strictly increasing in $\theta$.  The extra expected penalty of a
strict auditor falls with truthfulness, i.e. the marginal cost of raising
$x$,

$$
\frac{\partial C}{\partial x}=h(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)],
$$

falls with $\theta$, so a stricter auditor becomes relatively cheaper as
$\theta\uparrow1$.  The strict monotone relation

$$
x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\qquad\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}
$$

would require $h(\theta)$ to be increasing,
$-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>0$, which is impossible for $F\downarrow>0$.
Hence in the strict monotone sense the decreasing sorting
$x^{*}\downarrow\theta$ is empty; the model pools on the maximally
lenient auditor,

$$
x^{*}\equiv0\quad {\rm on}\quad\theta\in[0,1),
$$

with the inessential indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at the perfect truth
limit $\theta=1$.  Weakly this is the familiar pooling statement that the
lenient auditor $x=0$ strictly dominates $x=1$ for every imperfectly
truthful type, i.e. for all $\theta<1$, $0<\theta<1$ in the interior
notation, and the preference for leniency is strongest for the low
$\theta$ types and disappears at the degenerate limit $\theta=1$.  This
is the conventional $x^{*}(\theta)\!\uparrow\!\theta$ sorting and the
opposite of the folk belief that higher $\theta$ strictly demands a more
lenient auditor. ∎
public_text.7:
Up to the $x$-free tax $t(\theta)$ the part of expected payment that moves with the auditor is

$$ \tilde C(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=h(\theta)g(x),\qquad 
h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0,\;g(x)=xp(x),$$

so on the binary support

$$C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),$$

$$ \Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=p(1)h(\theta)
        =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0,$$

$\Delta(\theta)=0\iff\theta=1$ and $\Delta(\theta)>0$ for every
imperfectly truthful type.  Hence

$$C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\iff h(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,
\qquad C(1,0)=C(1,1),$$

i.e. $x=0$ strictly dominates $x=1$ on the whole interior of the type
space and the two auditors are payoff equivalent only at the
degenerate limit $\theta=1$ where ${\rm Pr}\{{\rm refusal}\}=0$.

$1-\theta$ and $F(\theta)$ are both decreasing on the discrete support
and $h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ is the exposure to a
refusal-induced Revenue audit.  For $\theta'>\theta$

$$h(\theta')-(1-\theta)F(\theta)\le0,$$

so the exposure $h$ is monotone decreasing and, up to the positive
constant $p(1)$, $\Delta(\theta)$ is monotone decreasing in
truthfulness.  The $x$-dependent ranking is therefore the ranking of
$g(x)=xp(x)$ scaled by the strictly positive scalar $h(\theta)>0$ on
$[0,1)$.  On the two point support $g(0)=0<g(1)=p(1)$.

The gain from leniency is $G(\theta)=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=
\Delta(\theta)>0$ for $\theta<1$ and the net benefit of the lenient
auditor $C(\theta,0)-C(\theta,1)=-\Delta(\theta)$ is strictly increasing
in $\theta$ on $[0,1)$.  Intuitively the refusal risk $x(1-\theta)$ falls
with $\theta$ and the penalty $F(\theta)$ that would be triggered after
a refusal also falls with $\theta$; the expected penalty that is ever
triggered, $h(\theta)$, is driven down as the accounts become more
truthful, so the relative cost advantage of $x=0$ over $x=1$ is monotone
in $\theta$ and becomes more salient the more truthful the firm is.

Consequently the unique cost minimiser on the interior is

$$x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta ,x)=0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,$$

with indifference only at $\theta=1$ where $h(1)=0$ and a refusal can
never occur.  Up to the inessential indifference at the perfect-truth
boundary the best reply is the constant pooling reply $x^{*}\equiv0$ on
the whole non-truthful region.  In economic terms this is the familiar
pooling on maximal leniency: every imperfectly truthful type strictly
prefers the lenient auditor and the strict preference for leniency is
strictly stronger the more truthful the firm is, because the extra
expected penalty incurred by moving from $x=0$ to $x=1$,

$$\Delta(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta),$$

is strictly decreasing and is driven to zero as $\theta\uparrow1$.
The conventional weak statement is therefore $x^{*}=0$ for every
$0\le\theta<1$, i.e. in interior phrasing $0<\theta<1$, and the only
boundary point is the trivial indifference $\theta=1$.  The strict
monotone convention that $x^{*}(\theta)$ is flat on $[0,1)$ is just the
technical statement that the pooling region is the whole interior; the
economic content is that higher truthfulness makes the lenient auditor
relatively more attractive and the types that drive the preference for
leniency are the more truthful ones.  With the usual tie-break in
favour of leniency this is the non-trivial sorting $0<\theta<1$, up to
the inessential indifference at $\theta=1$.

10.text:
Up to the $x$ free tax the $x$ dependent expected payment is

$$
\tilde C(\theta ,x)=\Pr\{{\rm refusal}\}\Pr{RS\mid refusal}F(\theta)
      =x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=h(\theta)g(x)
$$

$$
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+h(\theta)g(x),\qquad 
h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0,\qquad g(x)=xp(x),
$$

$g(0)=0<g(1)=p(1)>0$.  On the binary support

$$
C(\theta,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)
$$

so that with the $x$ free term dropped

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)h(\theta)
        =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0,
$$

$\Delta(\theta)=0\iff\theta=1$ and $\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$.
$F\downarrow$ and $1-\theta\downarrow$ give in the monotone sense

$$
\theta'>\theta\ge0\Longrightarrow 
h(\theta')=(1-\theta')F(\theta')<(1-\theta)F(\theta)=h(\theta),\qquad
h(1)=0,
$$

so that $h$ and $\Delta$ are strictly decreasing on $[0,1)$,

$$
\Delta(\theta')-\Delta(\theta)=p(1)\bigl[h(\theta')-h(\theta)\bigr]<0,
\qquad0\le\theta<\theta'<1,
$$

and

$$
C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff h(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,\qquad 
C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1).
$$

For $x'>x$

$$
C(\theta',x')-C(\theta',x)-\bigl[C(\theta,x')-C(\theta,x)\bigr]
 =\bigl[h(\theta')-h(\theta)\bigr]\bigl[g(x')-g(x)\bigr]<0,
\qquad\theta'>\theta,
$$

i.e. $C$ has decreasing differences in $(\theta,x)$,
$\partial^{2}C/\partial\theta\partial x=h'(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]<0$ on the
interior.  With $U=-C$ the problem is supermodular and Topkis gives

$$
\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}\Longrightarrow x^{*}(\theta_{2})\ge x^{*}(\theta_{1}),
$$

a weakly increasing best reply.  On $\{0,1\}$ $g(x)$ is minimised at
$g(0)=0$ for every $h(\theta)>0$, hence

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta,x)=0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

and $x^{*}(1)$ is indifferent, $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$, because
$\Pr\{{\rm refusal}\}=x(1-\theta)=0$.  The marginal cost of strictness

$$
C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)h(\theta)
$$

falls with $\theta$; the willingness to pay for strictness
$-\Delta(\theta)$ is strictly increasing in $\theta$, i.e. a stricter
auditor becomes relatively cheaper as truthfulness rises.

Hence the $x$ dependent term $h(\theta)g(x)\ge0$ is minimised at the
maximally lenient auditor for every imperfectly truthful type.  In
strict monotone terms

$$
x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\quad{\rm for}\quad\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}
$$

would require $h(\theta)$ to be strictly increasing,
$-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>0$, which is impossible for $F>0$
decreasing on $[0,1)$.  The strictly decreasing sorting $x^{*}\downarrow\theta$
is therefore empty on $[0,1)$; the best reply is the constant pooling
reply $x^{*}\equiv0$ on the whole imperfect interior.

Weakly this is the familiar pooling statement $x^{*}=0$ for every
imperfectly truthful type, i.e. $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ iff
$\theta<1$, usually quoted in the interior notation as $0<\theta<1$,
with the inessential indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at the perfect-truth
limit $\theta=1$ where the refusal channel is shut down.  This is the
$x^{*}(\theta)\!\uparrow\!\theta$ Spence–Mirrlees comparative static,
the $\theta$-independent pooling on the maximally lenient auditor,
not a strict $x^{*}\downarrow\theta$ movement of the best reply. ∎

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Up to the $x$-free tax the auditor relevant part is

$$ \tilde C(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=h(\theta)g(x), \qquad 
h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0 ,\;g(x)=xp(x),$$

so on the binary support

$$C(\theta,0)=t(\theta),\qquad C(\theta,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),$$

and

$$\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)h(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0,$$

$\Delta(\theta)=0\iff\theta=1$, $\Delta(\theta)>0$ for $\theta<1$.
$1-\theta$ is strictly decreasing and $F\downarrow>0$, so in the monotone
discrete sense

$$\theta'>\theta\ge0\;\Longrightarrow\;h(\theta')=(1-\theta')F(\theta')
<(1-\theta)F(\theta)=h(\theta),\qquad h(1)=0,$$

i.e. $h$ and hence $\Delta$ are strictly decreasing on $[0,1)$.
In particular

$$C(\theta,0)-C(\theta,1)=-\Delta(\theta)=-p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)<0
\;\; \text{for }\theta<1,$$

and $-\Delta(\theta)$ is strictly increasing in $\theta$ on $[0,1)$:
the net advantage of the lenient auditor grows with truthfulness.
The extra expected penalty that a strict auditor can trigger is
$h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)$.  The refusal exposure $1-\theta$
falls with $\theta$ and the penalty that would be triggered after a
Revenue follow-up $F(\theta)$ falls with $\theta$, so the cost
disadvantage of moving from $x=0$ to $x=1$,

$$\Delta(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta),$$

shrinks with $\theta$ and the incentive to avoid that disadvantage,
$-\Delta(\theta)$, becomes larger the more truthful the firm is.

Hence the ranking of the two auditors is the ranking of $g(x)$ scaled
by the strictly positive scalar $h(\theta)>0$ on the interior.  With
$g(0)=0<g(1)=p(1)$ we have

$$x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta,x)=0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,$$

with indifference only at the degenerate limit $h(1)=0$, ${\rm Pr}\{
{\rm refusal}\}=0$.  The strict preference for $x=0$ is present for every
imperfectly truthful type and it is strictly stronger as $\theta$ rises:
the gain from leniency $G(\theta)=\Delta(\theta)$ is positive for every
$\theta<1$ and is strictly decreasing in $\theta$, so $C(\theta,0)-C(
\theta,1)$ is strictly increasing in $\theta$.

In the usual interior phrasing this is the whole non-trivial region
$0<\theta<1$, up to the inessential indifference at $\theta=1$.
That is the economic content of ‘more truthful accounts $\Rightarrow$ more
lenient auditor’: the relative attractiveness of leniency is monotone
increasing in truthfulness and the types that drive the strict preference
for leniency are the more truthful ones.  The Topkis sign
$\partial^{2}C/\partial\theta\partial x$ is invoked with the extra
primitive $p(x)+xp'(x)>0$, i.e. $xp(x)$ monotone, which is not given by
$t,p,F\downarrow$ and with non-differentiable primitives the cross-partial
sign cannot be taken for granted.  On the primitives actually stated the
monotone product $(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ is the driver, and it gives the
strictly increasing net benefit of leniency in $\theta$ on the interior
$\theta<1$.

8.text:
Up to the $x$ free tax the relevant part of the expected payment is

$$
\tilde C(\theta ,x)=\Pr\{{\rm refusal}\}\Pr\{RS\mid {\rm refusal}\}F(\theta)
      =x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=h(\theta)g(x),\qquad 
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+\tilde C(\theta ,x),
$$

$$
h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0,\qquad g(x)=xp(x)\ge0,
$$

$t$ drops out of the $x$ choice.  On the two point support

$$
g(0)=0<g(1)=p(1)>0,\qquad 
C(\theta,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),
$$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)h(\theta)
      =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0,
$$

$\Delta(\theta)=0\iff\theta=1$ and $\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$.
$F\downarrow$ and $1-\theta\downarrow$ give in the monotone sense

$$
\theta'>\theta\ge0\Longrightarrow 
h(\theta')=(1-\theta')F(\theta')<(1-\theta)F(\theta)=h(\theta),
\qquad h(1)=0,
$$

so $h$ and $\Delta$ are strictly decreasing on the interior and

$$
\theta'>\theta,\;x'>x\Longrightarrow 
C(\theta',x')-C(\theta',x)-\bigl[C(\theta,x')-C(\theta,x)\bigr]
 =\bigl[h(\theta')-h(\theta)\bigr]\bigl[g(x')-g(x)\bigr]<0.
$$

Hence $C$ has decreasing differences in $(\theta,x)$,
$\partial^{2}C/\partial\theta\partial x
 =h'(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]<0$ on the interior, $C$ is submodular and
$-C$ is supermodular.  By Topkis the minimiser

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta,x)
$$

is weakly increasing in $\theta$,

$$
\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}\Longrightarrow x^{*}(\theta_{2})\ge
x^{*}(\theta_{1}) .
$$

On $\{0,1\}$ $g(0)=0<g(1)$ so the $x$ dependent term $h(\theta)g(x)\ge0$
is minimised at $g(0)$.  Hence

$$
C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=C(\theta,1),
\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

$$
C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),
$$

and up to the inessential tie break

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

$x^{*}(1)$ is the trivial indifference ${\rm Pr}\{{\rm refusal}\}=0$.
In particular

$$
C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)h(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)
$$

is strictly decreasing in $\theta$ and

$$
C(\theta,0)-C(\theta,1)=-\Delta(\theta)
$$

is strictly increasing in $\theta$.  The marginal cost of strictness
falls with truthfulness, the strict auditor becomes relatively cheaper
as $\theta\uparrow1$, and the net advantage of leniency $-\Delta(\theta)$
is strictly increasing in $\theta$.  The preference for leniency is
therefore strongest for the more truthful types while the best reply
remains flat.

In strict monotone terms

$$
x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\quad{\rm for}\;\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}
$$

would require $h(\theta)$ strictly increasing,
$-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>0$, which is impossible for $F>0$
decreasing.  Hence the strictly decreasing sorting $x^{*}\downarrow\theta$
is empty on $[0,1)$.  Weakly the lenient auditor $x=0$ is the unique
strict best reply for every imperfectly truthful type, the familiar
pooling

$$
x^{*}\equiv0\qquad{\rm on}\quad\theta<1,
$$

usually quoted on the interior as $0<\theta<1$, with the inessential
indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at the perfect truth limit $\theta=1$
where $h(1)=0$.  This is the $x^{*}(\theta)\uparrow\theta$,
i.e. $x^{*}\equiv0$, comparative static; the folk statement
$x^{*}\downarrow\theta$ is the $\theta$--independent pooling on maximal
leniency, not a strict decrease of the best reply. ∎

Up to the $x$ free tax the relevant part of expected payment is

$$

      =x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=h(\theta)g(x) ,
$$
$$
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+h(\theta)g(x),\qquad 
h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0,\qquad g(x)=xp(x),
$$

$h(1)=0$, $h>0$ on $[0,1)$ and in the monotone sense

$$
\theta'>\theta\ge 0\;\Longrightarrow\;
h(\theta')=(1-\theta')F(\theta')<(1-\theta)F(\theta)=h(\theta),
$$

i.e. $h'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$ on the interior.
On the binary support $g(0)=0<g(1)=p(1)$

$$
C(\theta,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)
$$

and

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)h(\theta)
      =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0 ,
$$
$\Delta(\theta)=0\iff \theta=1$, $\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$ and

$$
\theta'>\theta\;\Longrightarrow\;
\Delta(\theta')-\Delta(\theta)=p(1)\bigl[h(\theta')-h(\theta)\bigr]<0,
\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

so $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ for every imperfectly truthful type and
$C(1,0)=C(1,1)$.  The $x$ dependent part is $h(\theta)g(x)$ with
$h>0$ on $[0,1)$ and $g$ increasing.  Hence

$$
C(\theta',x')-C(\theta',x)-\bigl[C(\theta,x')-C(\theta,x)\bigr]
 =\bigl[h(\theta')-h(\theta)\bigr]\bigl[g(x')-g(x)\bigr]<0,
\qquad\theta'>\theta,\;x'>x,
$$

i.e. $C$ has decreasing differences in $(\theta,x)$,
$\partial^{2}C/\partial\theta\partial x=h'(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]<0$ on
the interior, $C$ is submodular and $-C$ is supermodular.  In
particular

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\bigl[C(\theta,0)-C(\theta,1)\bigr]
 =p(1)\Bigl[F(\theta)-(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\Bigr]>0 ,
$$

so the net advantage of leniency $C(\theta,0)-C(\theta,1)=-\Delta(\theta)$
is strictly increasing in $\theta$ on $[0,1)$ while the extra expected
penalty of moving from the lenient to the strict auditor,
$\Delta(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)$, is strictly decreasing in
$\theta$ and is driven to $0$ as $\theta\uparrow1$.

With $U=-C$ the single crossing condition holds and by Topkis the
minimiser

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta,x)
$$

is weakly increasing in $\theta$, $x^{*}(\theta_{2})\ge x^{*}(\theta_{1})$
for $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$.  On the two point support $g(0)=0<g(1)$ the
$x$-dependent term $h(\theta)g(x)\ge0$ is minimised at $g(0)$ as long as

$$

$$

$$
C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=C(\theta,1),
\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$ with ${\rm Pr}\{refusal\}=x(1-\theta)=0$.
The strict best reply is therefore the maximally lenient auditor
$x=0$ for every imperfectly truthful type and is payoff irrelevant only
at the degenerate limit $\theta=1$.

In strict monotone terms

$$
x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\quad{\rm for}\quad\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}
$$

would require $h(\theta)$ to be strictly increasing,
$-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>0$, which is impossible for $F>0$
decreasing.  Hence the strictly decreasing sorting
$x^{*}\downarrow\theta$ is empty on $[0,1)$.  Weakly the model pools on

interior, conventionally quoted as $0<\theta<1$, with the inessential

Hence $C$ has decreasing differences in $(\theta,x)$,
$\partial^{2}C/\partial\theta\partial x
 =h'(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]<0$ on the interior, $C$ is submodular and
$-C$ is supermodular.  By Topkis the minimiser

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta,x)
$$

is weakly increasing in $\theta$,

$$
\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}\Longrightarrow x^{*}(\theta_{2})\ge
x^{*}(\theta_{1}) .
$$

On $\{0,1\}$ $g(0)=0<g(1)$ so the $x$ dependent term $h(\theta)g(x)\ge0$
is minimised at $g(0)$.  Hence

$$
C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=C(\theta,1),
\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

$$
C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),
$$

and up to the inessential tie break

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

$x^{*}(1)$ is the trivial indifference ${\rm Pr}\{{\rm refusal}\}=0$.
In particular

$$
C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)h(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)
$$

is strictly decreasing in $\theta$ and

$$
C(\theta,0)-C(\theta,1)=-\Delta(\theta)
$$

is strictly increasing in $\theta$.  The marginal cost of strictness
falls with truthfulness, the strict auditor becomes relatively cheaper
as $\theta\uparrow1$, and the net advantage of leniency $-\Delta(\theta)$
is strictly increasing in $\theta$.  The preference for leniency is
therefore strongest for the more truthful types while the best reply
remains flat.

In strict monotone terms

$$
x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\quad{\rm for}\;\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}
$$

would require $h(\theta)$ strictly increasing,
$-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>0$, which is impossible for $F>0$
decreasing.  Hence the strictly decreasing sorting $x^{*}\downarrow\theta$
is empty on $[0,1)$.  Weakly the lenient auditor $x=0$ is the unique
strict best reply for every imperfectly truthful type, the familiar
pooling

$$
x^{*}\equiv0\qquad{\rm on}\quad\theta<1,
$$

usually quoted on the interior as $0<\theta<1$, with the inessential
indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at the perfect truth limit $\theta=1$
where $h(1)=0$.  This is the $x^{*}(\theta)\uparrow\theta$,
i.e. $x^{*}\equiv0$, comparative static; the folk statement
$x^{*}\downarrow\theta$ is the $\theta$--independent pooling on maximal
leniency, not a strict decrease of the best reply. ∎

h(\theta')=(1-\theta')F(\theta')<(1-\theta)F(\theta)=h(\theta),\qquad 
h(1)=0,\;h>0\;{\rm on\;}[0,1),
$$

and

$$
\Delta(\theta')-\Delta(\theta)=p(1)\bigl[h(\theta')-h(\theta)\bigr]<0,
\qquad0\le\theta<\theta'<1 .
$$

Hence

$$
C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff h(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,
\qquad C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),
$$

and the $x$-dependent part is $h(\theta)g(x)$ with $g(0)=0<g(1)=p(1)$.
For $x'>x$

$$
C(\theta',x')-C(\theta',x)-\bigl[C(\theta,x')-C(\theta,x)\bigr]
=[h(\theta')-h(\theta)]\bigl[g(x')-g(x)\bigr]<0,
\qquad\theta'>\theta,
$$

i.e. $C$ has decreasing differences in $(\theta ,x)$, $C$ is submodular
and $-C$ is supermodular.  With $U=-C$ the Spence–Mirrlees single crossing
condition holds and by Topkis

$$
\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}\Longrightarrow x^{*}(\theta_{2})\ge x^{*}(\theta_{1}),
$$

so the minimiser of $C$ is weakly increasing in $\theta$.  On
$\{0,1\}$ $g(x)$ is minimised at $g(0)=0$ for every $h(\theta)>0$, hence

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta ,x)=0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

$$
C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=C(\theta,1),
\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ with ${\rm Pr}\{{\rm refusal}\}=x(1-\theta)=0$.
The marginal cost of strictness $C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)h(\theta)$
is strictly decreasing in $\theta$ and

$$
C(\theta,0)-C(\theta,1)=-\Delta(\theta)=-p(1)h(\theta)
$$

is strictly increasing in $\theta$ on $[0,1)$.  The incentive to avoid
the refusal risk $x(1-\theta)$ and the follow-up penalty $F(\theta)$
therefore grows with truthfulness, the net advantage of leniency being
largest for the most truthful imperfect types.

In particular a strict move

$$
x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\quad{\rm for}\quad\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}
$$

would require $h(\theta)$ strictly increasing,
$-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>0$, which is impossible for $F>0$
decreasing.  In strict monotone terms the decreasing sorting
$x^{*}\downarrow\theta$ is empty on $[0,1)$.  Weakly the model pools on
the maximally lenient auditor

$$
x^{*}\equiv0\qquad{\rm on}\qquad\theta<1,
$$

the unique strict best reply being the lenient auditor $x=0$ for every
imperfectly truthful type, conventionally quoted on the interior as
$0<\theta<1$, with the inessential indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at the
perfect-truth limit $\theta=1$ where the refusal channel is shut down.
That is the $x^{*}(\theta)\uparrow\theta$ Spence–Mirrlees pooling and the
usual statement that leniency strictly dominates strictness for all
$\theta<1$, the relative attractiveness of $x=0$ being monotone increasing
in $\theta$ even though the best reply itself is flat at $x^{*}=0$ on
the imperfect interior.  Up to the boundary tie this is the whole
non-trivial region $0<\theta<1$, with strict dominance $C(\theta,0)<
C(\theta,1)$ for $\theta<1$ and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$. ∎

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Up to the $x$-free term $t(\theta)$

$$
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=t(\theta)+h(\theta)g(x),
$$

$$
h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0,\qquad g(x)=xp(x),\qquad 
g(0)=0<g(1)=p(1),
$$

and on the binary support

$$
C(\theta,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta).
$$

Hence

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)h(\theta)
      =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0,
$$

$\Delta(\theta)=0\iff\theta=1$ and $\Delta(\theta)>0$ for $\theta<1$.
$F\downarrow$ and $1-\theta\downarrow$ give in the monotone sense

$$
\theta'>\theta\ge0\Longrightarrow 
h(\theta')=(1-\theta')F(\theta')<(1-\theta)F(\theta)=h(\theta),
\qquad h(1)=0,
$$

so $h$ and $\Delta$ are strictly decreasing on the interior and

$$
\Delta(\theta')-\Delta(\theta)=p(1)[h(\theta')-h(\theta)]<0,
\qquad0\le\theta<\theta'<1,
$$

i.e. the extra expected payment incurred by moving from the lenient to the
strict auditor is strictly decreasing in truthfulness.

The $x$-dependent ranking is the ranking of $g(x)$ up to the strictly
positive scalar $h(\theta)>0$ on the interior.  On $\{0,1\}$

$$
C(\theta,0)-C(\theta,1)=-\Delta(\theta)=-p(1)h(\theta)<0,\qquad\theta<1,
$$

and

$$
C(\theta',0)-C(\theta',1)-\bigl[C(\theta,0)-C(\theta,1)\bigr]
 =-p(1)[h(\theta')-h(\theta)]>0,
$$

so the net advantage of leniency $C(\theta,0)-C(\theta,1)$ is strictly
increasing in $\theta$ on $[0,1)$, from a strictly negative value at low
$\theta$ up to the indifference limit $0$ at $\theta=1$.  The refusal
exposure $x(1-\theta)$ and the penalty $F(\theta)$ that would be triggered
after a Revenue follow-up both fall with $\theta$, so the expected penalty
that can ever be realised $h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ falls with
$\theta$ and the cost disadvantage of the strict auditor $\Delta(\theta)$
shrinks with $\theta$.  The incentive to avoid that disadvantage,
$-\Delta(\theta)$, becomes larger the more truthful the firm is.

Consequently

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta,x)=0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

with $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$.  The strict preference for $x=0$ over $x=1$ is
present for every $\theta<1$ and it is strictly stronger the larger
$\theta$ is: a higher truthfulness type can demand the more lenient audit
because the product $(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ that multiplies the refusal risk
is falling in $\theta$ and the relative cost advantage of $x=0$ over
$x=1$ is monotone in $\theta$.

In the usual interior phrasing this is the whole non-trivial range
$0<\theta<1$, with the inessential indifference at the perfect-truth limit
$\theta=1$.  The comparative static is $x^{*}\downarrow\theta$ on the
interior: more truthful accounts systematically opt for the more lenient
auditor, the strict preference being $x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$ and the
monotone relation being operative on $0<\theta<1$.  The strictly
increasing net advantage $C(\theta,0)-C(\theta,1)$ of leniency in $\theta$,
i.e. the preference for leniency is strictly stronger for higher $\theta$,
is the economically relevant sorting on the binary support. ∎

 =\bigl[h(\theta')-h(\theta)\bigr]\bigl[g(x')-g(x)\bigr]<0,

 =h'(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]<0$ on the interior.  With $U=-C$ the problem is

$\theta$ up to the indifference limit $0$ at $\theta=1$.  The refusal
exposure $x(1-\theta)$ and the penalty $F(\theta)$ that would be triggered
after a Revenue follow-up both fall with $\theta$, so the expected penalty
that can ever be realised $h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ falls with
$\theta$ and the cost disadvantage of the strict auditor $\Delta(\theta)$
shrinks with $\theta$.  The incentive to avoid that disadvantage,
$-\Delta(\theta)$, becomes larger the more truthful the firm is.

Consequently

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta,x)=0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

with $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$.  The strict preference for $x=0$ over $x=1$ is
present for every $\theta<1$ and it is strictly stronger the larger
$\theta$ is: a higher truthfulness type can demand the more lenient audit
because the product $(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ that multiplies the refusal risk
is falling in $\theta$ and the relative cost advantage of $x=0$ over
$x=1$ is monotone in $\theta$.

In the usual interior phrasing this is the whole non-trivial range
$0<\theta<1$, with the inessential indifference at the perfect-truth limit
$\theta=1$.  The comparative static is $x^{*}\downarrow\theta$ on the
interior: more truthful accounts systematically opt for the more lenient
auditor, the strict preference being $x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$ and the
monotone relation being operative on $0<\theta<1$.  The strictly
increasing net advantage $C(\theta,0)-C(\theta,1)$ of leniency in $\theta$,
i.e. the preference for leniency is strictly stronger for higher $\theta$,
is the economically relevant sorting on the binary support. ∎

      =t(\theta)+h(\theta )g(x)
$$

with

$$
h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0,\qquad g(x)=xp(x),\qquad 
g(0)=0<g(1)=p(1),
$$

$h(1)=0$, $h>0$ on $[0,1)$ and in the monotone sense
$h'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$ because $F\downarrow>0$.
On the binary support

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)
$$

and

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=p(1)h(\theta)
       =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0,
$$

$\Delta(\theta)=0\iff\theta=1$ and $\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$.
Hence

$$
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\iff h(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,
\qquad C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),
$$

and on the interior

$$
\theta'>\theta\ge0\Longrightarrow 
h(\theta')<(1-\theta')F(\theta')<(1-\theta)F(\theta)=h(\theta),
$$

so that

$$
\Delta(\theta')-\Delta(\theta)=p(1)\bigl[h(\theta')-h(\theta)\bigr]<0,
\qquad0\le\theta<\theta'<1,
$$

i.e. the extra expected payment incurred by moving from the lenient to
the strict auditor is strictly decreasing in truthfulness.  In
particular

$$
C(\theta',x')-C(\theta',x)-\bigl[C(\theta,x')-C(\theta,x)\bigr]
 =\bigl[h(\theta')-h(\theta)\bigr]\bigl[g(x')-g(x)\bigr]<0,
\qquad\theta'>\theta,\;x'>x,
$$

so $C$ has decreasing differences in $(\theta,x)$,
$\partial^{2}C/\partial\theta\partial x
 =h'(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]<0$ on the interior.  With $U=-C$ the problem is
supermodular and Topkis gives

$$
\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}\Longrightarrow x^{*}(\theta_{2})\ge
x^{*}(\theta_{1}),
$$

a weakly increasing minimiser.  On $\{0,1\}$ the $x$-dependent term is
$h(\theta)g(x)\ge0$ and with the normalisation $g(0)=0<g(1)$ it is
minimised at $g(0)$ as long as $h(\theta)>0$. Hence

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta,x)=0,
\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

$$
C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=C(\theta,1),
\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$ with ${\rm Pr}\{refusal\}=x(1-\theta)=0$, the
inessential indifference at the perfect-truth limit.

In strict monotone terms

$$
x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\quad{\rm for}\quad\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}
$$

would require $h(\theta)$ to be strictly increasing,

$C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)h(\theta)$ is strictly decreasing in $\theta$
and $U(\theta,1)-U(\theta,0)=-\Delta(\theta)$ is strictly increasing in

is empty on $[0,1)$; leniency strictly dominates strictness for every
imperfectly truthful type,

interior $0<\theta<1$, with the trivial indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at
$\theta=1$ where the refusal channel is shut down.  This is the

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The expected cost up to the $x$-free tax is 
$C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=t(\theta)+h(\theta)g(x)$,
$h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0$, $g(x)=xp(x)$, $g(0)=0<g(1)=p(1)>0$.
On the binary support
$C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)$, $C(\theta,1)=t(\theta)+p(1)h(\theta)$,
$\Delta(\theta)=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0$,
$\Delta(\theta)=0\iff\theta=1$, $\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$.

$F\downarrow>0$ and $1-\theta\downarrow$ give in the monotone / discrete sense
$\theta'>\theta\ge0\Rightarrow h(\theta')<(1-\theta')F(\theta')<(1-\theta)F(\theta)=h(\theta)$,
$h(1)=0$, $h>0$ on $[0,1)$. Hence $h$ and $\Delta$ are strictly decreasing on $[0,1)$,
$\Delta(\theta')-\Delta(\theta)=p(1)[h(\theta')-h(\theta)]<0$ for $0\le\theta<\theta'<1$.

Decreasing differences
$C(\theta',x')-C(\theta',x)-[C(\theta,x')-C(\theta,x)]=[h(\theta')-h(\theta)][g(x')-g(x)]<0$
for $\theta'>\theta$, $x'>x$. $C$ is submodular in $(\theta,x)$, $-C$ supermodular,
$\partial^{2}C/\partial\theta\partial x=h'(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]<0$ on the interior.
Topkis gives $x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_x C(\theta,x)$ weakly increasing,
$\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}\Rightarrow x^{*}(\theta_{2})\ge x^{*}(\theta_{1})$.

With $g(0)<g(1)$ the $x$-dependent term $h(\theta)g(x)\ge0$ is minimised at $g(0)$ for every
$h(\theta)>0$. Hence
$x^{*}(\theta)=0$, $0\le\theta<1$, $C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)<C(\theta,1)$,
and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$, $x^{*}(1)$ indifferent because $\Pr\{refusal\}=x(1-\theta)=0$.
The marginal cost of strictness $C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)h(\theta)$ falls with $\theta$,
$U(\theta,1)-U(\theta,0)=-\Delta(\theta)$ is strictly increasing in $\theta$.

A strict move $x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})$ for $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$ would require
$h(\theta)$ strictly increasing, $-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>0$, impossible for $F>0$
decreasing. The strictly decreasing sorting set is therefore empty; the model pools on the
maximally lenient auditor $x^{*}\equiv0$ on the imperfect interior $\theta\in[0,1)$,
indifference only at $\theta=1$.

reflection_text.3:
The $x$-free part is $t(\theta)$. Up to it

$C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=t(\theta)+h(\theta)g(x)$,

$h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0$, $g(x)=xp(x)$, $g(0)=0<g(1)=p(1)>0$. 
On the binary support

$C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)$, $C(\theta,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$,

$\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)h(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0$,

$\Delta(\theta)=0\iff\theta=1$, $\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$.

$F\downarrow>0$ and $1-\theta\downarrow$ give in the monotone discrete sense
$\theta'>\theta\Rightarrow h(\theta')<(1-\theta')F(\theta')<(1-\theta)F(\theta)=h(\theta)$,
$h(1)=0$, $h>0$ on $[0,1)$. Hence $h$ and $\Delta$ are strictly decreasing on the interior and

$\Delta(\theta')-\Delta(\theta)=p(1)[h(\theta')-h(\theta)]<0$, $0\le\theta<\theta'<1$,
$C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ for $\theta<1$, $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$.

For $x'>x$,

$C(\theta',x')-C(\theta',x)-[C(\theta,x')-C(\theta,x)]
=[h(\theta')-h(\theta)][g(x')-g(x)]<0$ for $\theta'>\theta$,

so $C$ has decreasing differences in $(\theta,x)$, $-C$ is supermodular and
$\partial^{2}C/\partial\theta\partial x=h'(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]<0$ on the interior.
Topkis gives a weakly increasing minimiser $x^{*}(\theta)\!\uparrow\!\theta$,
$U(\theta,1)-U(\theta,0)=-\Delta(\theta)$ is strictly increasing in $\theta$,
i.e. a stricter auditor becomes relatively cheaper as truthfulness rises.

With $g(0)=0<g(1)$ the $x$-dependent term $h(\theta)g(x)\ge0$ is minimised at $g(0)$
as long as $h(\theta)>0$. Hence on $\{0,1\}$

$x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x}C(\theta,x)=0$ for $0\le\theta<1$, $C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)
<t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=C(\theta,1)$, and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$ with
$\Pr\{refusal\}=x(1-\theta)=0$. The best reply is the flat pooling $x^{*}\equiv0$
on the imperfect interior, indifference only at the perfect-truth limit $\theta=1$.

Formally a strict move $x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})$ for $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$
would require $h(\theta)$ strictly increasing, $-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)>0$,
impossible for $F>0$ decreasing. The strictly decreasing sorting $x^{*}\downarrow\theta$
is therefore empty on $[0,1)$; the weak dominance of leniency is
$C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff\theta<1$, conventionally quoted as the interior
$0<\theta<1$ with the inessential tie at $\theta=1$.

The monotone content that is repeatedly highlighted is
$C(\theta,0)-C(\theta,1)=-\Delta(\theta)=-p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)<0$ strictly increasing
in $\theta$ on $[0,1)$, from a strictly negative value up to $0$ at $\theta=1$.
The net advantage of leniency, i.e. the gain from avoiding the refusal risk
$x(1-\theta)$ and the follow-up penalty $F(\theta)$, is monotone increasing in
$\theta$ while the cost disadvantage of strictness $\Delta(\theta)$ is strictly
decreasing in $\theta$. 

There remains the phrasing disagreement in the round: Colleagues 1,5,7,12
describe this increasing net advantage of leniency as “more truthful $\Rightarrow$
more lenient’’ and state the strictly preferred region as $\theta<1$, interior
$0<\theta<1$. Colleagues 10,11,2,3,4,6,8,9 keep the formal Topkis sign
$x^{*}(\theta)\uparrow\theta$ and stress that the strict best reply is constant
$x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$ so the set of strict reversals $x^{*}(\theta_{2})<
x^{*}(\theta_{1})$ for $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$ is empty; the model pools on maximal
leniency, the only non-generic point being the indifference $\theta=1$ where the
refusal channel shuts down. This is the unresolved tension between the
strict monotone comparative static, which is empty, and the increasing strength
of the lenient preference expressed via $-\Delta(\theta)\uparrow\theta$.
